title: Psalm 135: Praise the God Who Acts, Not the Idols Who Can't
summary: A call to praise summons the servants in the LORD's house to celebrate his goodness, his choice of Israel, and his supremacy over all gods. The psalm recounts his power in the storm, in the plagues on Egypt, and in the defeat of the kings east of the Jordan, then mocks the idols of the nations as silver and gold that cannot speak, see, or hear. It closes by calling every part of Israel to bless the LORD who dwells in Jerusalem.
story: Psalm 135 picks up where the Songs of Ascents left off. Psalm 134 called the servants who stand in the LORD's house to bless him; Psalm 135 opens by addressing the same people, those “who stand in the house of the LORD” (verse 2), and gives them a whole song of reasons. It then prepares for Psalm 136, which retells much of the same history (creation, the exodus, Sihon and Og, the gift of the land) with a refrain after every line. Together the two psalms read like a pair: one proclaims what God has done, and the next gives thanks for it. Both belong to Book V of the Psalter (Psalms 107 to 150), which many scholars read as the Psalter's answer to the exile, a collection that teaches a humbled people to praise again.
historical:
The psalm has no superscription naming an author or occasion. It opens and closes with Hallelujah, a Hebrew call meaning praise the LORD. Its most striking feature is how much of it draws on other Scripture. Verses 15 to 18, on the idols, are nearly identical to Psalm 115:4-8. Verse 7, on clouds, lightning, and wind from God's storehouses, closely matches Jeremiah 10:13. Verse 14 repeats Deuteronomy 32:36, from the Song of Moses. Verse 4 echoes God's words at Sinai calling Israel his treasured possession (Exodus 19:5). Because of this dense borrowing, many scholars think the psalm was composed after the exile, in the period of the Second Temple, by a temple singer who knew the older texts well. Others note that shared liturgical language could have circulated in worship for a long time, so borrowing alone does not settle the date.

The history the psalm recites is Israel's founding story: the tenth plague on Egypt (Exodus 12), and the victories over Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan east of the Jordan (Numbers 21:21-35), followed by the gift of Canaan. For Israelites living under foreign rule after the exile, surrounded by the gods of the empires, recalling that the LORD had once overthrown Pharaoh and the kings of Canaan was a way of saying that he had not changed.
cultural:
Verse 7 carries a polemical edge that a first reader would feel. The Canaanites credited storms, rain, and lightning to Baal, the storm god whose worship tempted Israel for centuries. The psalm gives all of it to the LORD: he raises the clouds, makes lightning for the rain, and brings the wind out of his storehouses. The idol polemic of verses 15 to 18 targets the cult images found in every ancient temple, statues of wood overlaid with silver and gold. In Mesopotamia such images went through rituals intended to open their mouths and eyes so that the god would come to dwell in them. The psalm answers that they have mouths and eyes and ears and no breath at all, and it adds a sharp warning: those who make them and trust in them become like them.

The closing call in verses 19 and 20 names the groups gathered in the temple courts. The house of Israel is the whole people; the house of Aaron is the priests; the house of Levi is the Levites who served in the temple; and those who fear the LORD may be the whole worshiping community or, as some think, non-Israelites who had come to worship Israel's God. Psalm 115:9-11 uses a similar list without Levi.
literary: Psalm 135 is a hymn of praise built in a frame. Verses 1 to 4 call to praise and give the reason: the LORD is good and has chosen Israel. Verses 19 to 21 return to the call with a fourfold bless the LORD. Between them, verses 5 to 14 describe the LORD's greatness in creation and history, and verses 15 to 18 set the idols beside him. The contrast is the psalm's engine. The LORD does whatever pleases him in heaven, earth, and the seas (verse 6); the idols cannot speak, see, hear, or breathe. His name endures forever (verse 13); they are the work of human hands. Hallelujah stands at both ends like bookends.

outline.t: The call to praise the good God who chose Israel
The LORD above all gods, Lord of the storm
The exodus and the gift of the land
His name endures; he will vindicate his people
The idols that cannot speak, see, or hear
All Israel called to bless the LORD

doctrines.note: The psalm defines an idol by what it cannot do and warns that worshipers become like what they worship. Trust in a lifeless thing slowly makes a person lifeless in the same ways: unable to hear, see, or speak truly.

The LORD does all that pleases him in every realm, from the depths of the sea to the rise of the clouds and the fall of kings. His freedom is not arbitrary; it is exercised for his people's rescue and in keeping with his good name.

God chose Jacob as his own treasured possession, and the psalm grounds Israel's praise in that choice. His compassion on his servants in verse 14 is covenant faithfulness, the loyalty of a God who has bound himself to a people.

words.note: Segullah, treasured possession. The word describes a personal treasure, such as a king's private store of wealth (1 Chronicles 29:3 uses it of David's own gold and silver). God first used it of Israel at Sinai (Exodus 19:5). It says that Israel's worth lies in being chosen and held by God, not in its size or merit.

Atsav, idol. The word is related to a verb meaning to shape or fashion, and possibly to a word for pain or toil. It marks the idol as a crafted object. The psalm's point is that a god made by human hands can be no greater than the hands that made it.

Shem, name. In Hebrew thought a name stands for the person's revealed character and reputation. The LORD's name is lovely (verse 3) and endures forever (verse 13); praising his name means praising who he has shown himself to be in what he has done.

Halal, to praise. The imperative plural with the short divine name Yah gives Hallelujah, praise the LORD, which frames this psalm. The verb means to boast about or celebrate someone publicly. It is the root of the Hebrew name of the whole book of Psalms, Tehillim, praises.

christ: The New Testament takes up the psalm's contrast between the living God and lifeless idols. Paul praised the Thessalonians because they turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God (1 Thessalonians 1:9), and in Athens he argued that God does not dwell in temples made by hands (Acts 17:24-25). The psalm's warning that people become like what they worship has a positive counterpart in Paul: those who behold the Lord's glory are being transformed into his image (2 Corinthians 3:18). Christ is the true image of the invisible God, the one image that speaks, sees, hears, and breathes, and to worship him is to be made more fully alive. The psalm's hope that the LORD will vindicate his people and have compassion on his servants is, in the New Testament's reading, fulfilled in the cross and resurrection, where God acts decisively for his people as he once did at the exodus.

hard.q: Why does a hymn of praise celebrate the slaughter of kings and nations?
hard.a: Verses 10 to 12 praise God for striking down many nations and slaying mighty kings, and a modern reader can find that jarring in worship. The psalm is recalling specific events in Israel's story, above all the wars with Sihon and Og recorded in Numbers 21, where those kings refused Israel passage and came out to fight. Within the Old Testament these victories are presented as God's judgment on nations whose wickedness had reached its measure (compare Genesis 15:16) and as his faithfulness to a small, vulnerable people who could not have taken the land on their own. Christians read the conquest texts in different ways: some take them as a unique, limited act of divine judgment in a particular time; others stress the stylized, hyperbolic language of ancient war reports. What the psalm does not do is give any later reader license to call their own wars holy. Its focus is not on Israel's strength but on God's: he struck, he gave, and his name, not Israel's, endures.

questions: The psalm says that people become like what they trust. What do you trust most, and what is it making you into?
Why do you think the psalmist recites history instead of simply saying that God is great? What history would you recite?
The call to bless the LORD goes to the whole people, the priests, the Levites, and all who fear him. How does worship change when it is shared by very different people together?
